title: Smarter CTV Ads Through Creative Personalization
summary: CTV creative personalization is transforming how brands connect with audiences on the biggest screen in the home.
body_text: CTV creative personalization is transforming how brands connect with audiences on the biggest screen in the home. This guide explores how data-driven targeting, dynamic creative optimization, and interactive advertising formats are enabling more relevant, measurable, and impactful advertising across connected TV platforms heading into 2026. Key Takeaways Q: What makes CTV creative personalization different from traditional TV advertising? A: CTV creative personalization uses viewer data, behavioral signals, and real-time decisioning to serve tailored ad variations to specific audience segments—unlike linear TV, where every household sees the same commercial. Q: How does data facilitate personalized advertising without compromising privacy? A: Advertisers can rely on first-party data partnerships, contextual intelligence, and aggregated signals—strategies used by platforms like Perion—to deliver relevant CTV ads without individual user tracking or third-party cookies. Q: Why is dynamic creative optimization essential for scaling CTV campaigns? A: Dynamic creative optimization automatically assembles modular video elements based on audience data and performance signals, enabling hundreds of personalized ad combinations without the cost of producing each version manually. Q: How do interactive advertising formats improve CTV ad performance? A: Interactive advertising elements like QR codes and shoppable overlays turn passive viewers into active participants, generating richer engagement data and creating direct paths from the TV screen to conversion. Q: What role does location-based content play in CTV creative personalization? A: Location-based content allows brands to tailor CTV ads by region, weather, or store proximity—such as promoting snow gear in northern markets and patio furniture in the south within the same campaign. Q: How should advertisers measure the ROI of personalized CTV campaigns? A: Effective measurement combines exposed-vs.-control brand lift studies, multi-touch attribution, and creative-level performance breakdowns to connect CTV creative personalization directly to downstream business outcomes. Q: What trends will shape CTV creative personalization heading into 2026? A: AI-powered creative generation, shoppable CTV experiences, data clean room collaboration, and cross-screen creative sequencing will make personalized CTV advertising more automated, interactive, and integrated with the broader digital ecosystem. What Is CTV Creative Personalization? CTV creative personalization refers to the practice of tailoring ad content shown on connected television devices based on viewer data, context, and behavioral signals. Unlike traditional linear TV, where every household sees the same commercial, CTV allows advertisers to serve different creative variations to different audience segments, sometimes within the same program. Core Components of CTV Creative Personalization Audience segmentation: Dividing viewers into distinct groups based on demographics, interests, purchase history, or device data to deliver relevant messaging. Creative versioning: Producing multiple ad variations that differ in visuals, copy, calls to action, or product focus to match each segment’s preferences. Real-time decisioning: Using programmatic infrastructure to select and serve the right creative version at the moment of ad delivery. Contextual alignment: Matching ad content to the genre, time of day, or type of programming being watched. The distinction between CTV personalization and standard digital ad targeting is important. CTV operates in a lean-back, full-screen environment where viewer attention tends to be higher than on mobile or desktop. This makes the quality and relevance of the creative even more critical. A poorly targeted ad on a 55-inch screen is far more noticeable, and far more damaging to brand perception, than one buried in a mobile feed. Personalization on CTV also differs from addressable linear TV. While addressable TV can swap ads at the household level through cable set-top boxes, CTV personalization leverages IP-based targeting, first-party data integrations, and programmatic pipes that allow for greater granularity and faster iteration. Why Personalized Ads Are the Future of Television The shift from broadcast to streaming has fundamentally changed viewer expectations. Audiences accustomed to algorithmic content recommendations from platforms like Netflix and YouTube now expect advertising to feel equally relevant. Generic, one-size-fits-all commercials feel increasingly out of place in a personalized content environment. Consumer Demand for Relevance Research consistently shows that viewers respond more positively to ads that reflect their interests. According to a 2024 study by Innovid, personalized CTV ads generated 35% higher engagement rates compared to standard pre-roll. Viewers are not opposed to advertising; they are opposed to irrelevant advertising. Personalization bridges that gap. Advertiser Economics Favor Personalization Reduced waste: Serving tailored creatives means fewer impressions are spent on audiences unlikely to convert, improving cost efficiency. Higher conversion rates: Relevant messaging drives stronger response, whether that is a website visit, app download, or purchase. Better brand recall: Ads that resonate with a viewer’s context and interests are remembered longer and associated more positively with the brand. Competitive differentiation: Brands that personalize stand out against competitors still running generic spots. The economics are straightforward. CTV ad spend in the U.S. is projected to surpass $30 billion by 2026, according to eMarketer. As more dollars flow into the channel, the pressure to demonstrate measurable returns intensifies. Personalization is not a luxury; it is a performance requirement. Companies like Perion have recognized this trajectory and built their CTV advertising solutions around the principle that creative relevance directly correlates with campaign performance. Their approach combines audience intelligence with dynamic ad serving to help brands move beyond static TV spots. How Data Facilitates Personalized Advertising on CTV Platforms Data is the foundation of every personalized CTV campaign. Without reliable audience signals, personalization is guesswork. Understanding how data facilitates personalized advertising requires examining the types of data available, how they are collected, and how they inform creative decisions. Types of Data Used in CTV Personalization Data Type Source Use Case First-party data Advertiser CRM, website, app Retargeting existing customers with relevant offers Device graph data Cross-device identity providers Linking CTV viewers to their mobile and desktop activity Contextual data Content metadata, genre classification Aligning ads with programming mood and topic Geographic data IP-based geolocation Serving location-specific promotions or store locators Behavioral data Viewing history, ad interaction patterns Predicting interest categories and purchase intent Privacy-Compliant Data Strategies With third-party cookies absent from the CTV environment and privacy regulations tightening globally, advertisers must build personalization strategies on compliant data foundations. First-party data partnerships between brands and publishers offer one path forward. Contextual targeting, which requires no personal data at all, offers another. Perion’s advertising technology stack addresses this challenge by incorporating privacy-safe audience targeting that does not rely on individual user tracking. Their platform uses aggregated signals and contextual intelligence to deliver personalized ad experiences without compromising viewer privacy. The key takeaway is that data facilitates personalized advertising most effectively when it is accurate, consented, and activated in real time. Stale data or overly broad segments undermine the entire value proposition of personalization. The Role of Dynamic Creative Optimization (DCO) in CTV Dynamic creative optimization is the technology that makes CTV personalization scalable. Rather than manually producing dozens or hundreds of ad variations, DCO systems automatically assemble creative elements based on rules, data inputs, and performance signals. How DCO Works on CTV A DCO system typically operates with a modular creative framework. The advertiser provides a set of interchangeable components, and the system assembles the final ad in real time based on the viewer profile. Base template: A consistent brand framework that maintains visual identity across all variations. Swappable elements: Product images, headlines, offers, background scenes, voiceover scripts, and end cards that change per segment. Decision logic: Rules that determine which combination of elements to serve based on audience data, time of day, weather, or geography. Performance feedback loop: Real-time analytics that identify which combinations perform best, enabling automatic optimization. DCO vs. Traditional A/B Testing Traditional A/B testing compares two or three creative versions across a campaign. Dynamic creative optimization operates at a fundamentally different scale. A single DCO campaign might generate hundreds of unique combinations, each tailored to a specific audience micro-segment. The system continuously learns which combinations drive the strongest results and shifts delivery accordingly. This is particularly valuable on CTV, where production costs for video creative are higher than for display ads. DCO allows brands to maximize the return on their creative investment by ensuring every version of an ad is working as hard as possible. For advertisers working with platforms like Perion, dynamic creative optimization integrates directly into the programmatic buying process, enabling creative decisions and media decisions to happen simultaneously rather than in separate workflows. Crafting More Impactful Advertising with Tailored Messaging Personalization technology is only as effective as the creative strategy behind it. The most sophisticated targeting in the world cannot compensate for messaging that fails to resonate. Crafting impactful advertising on CTV requires a deliberate approach to message architecture, emotional tone, and audience-specific value propositions. Principles of Effective Personalized Creative Lead with relevance, not novelty: Personalization should make the ad feel more useful to the viewer, not more intrusive. The goal is a message that feels like it was made for them, not that it is watching them. Maintain brand consistency: Even as creative elements change across segments, the core brand identity, including visual style, tone, and positioning, should remain recognizable. Match message to funnel stage: A first-time viewer should see awareness-level messaging. A repeat visitor should see a product-specific offer or a call to action that reflects their prior engagement. Use emotional triggers appropriate to context: An ad served during a comedy special should feel different from one served during a documentary, even if the product is the same. Examples of Tailored Messaging Approaches Seasonal messaging: A retail brand swaps winter imagery for spring visuals automatically based on calendar triggers and regional weather data. Product-specific focus: An auto manufacturer highlights SUVs to suburban households and sedans to urban viewers based on geographic and demographic data. Loyalty recognition: An airline serves upgrade offers to frequent flyers and introductory fare promotions to new prospects. The result of these strategies is more impactful advertising that drives measurable business outcomes rather than simply accumulating impressions. When viewers see messaging that speaks to their specific situation, they are more likely to pay attention, remember the brand, and take action. Case Studies: From Interactive Advertising to Location-Based Content Theory matters, but results matter more. Several brands and technology providers have demonstrated the tangible benefits of CTV creative personalization through campaigns that combine interactive advertising elements with data-driven targeting. Interactive Advertising on CTV Interactive advertising formats on CTV allow viewers to engage directly with an ad using their remote control or second screen. These formats include clickable overlays, QR codes, shoppable product carousels, and trivia-style engagement units. The interactivity transforms a passive viewing experience into an active one, generating richer data signals and higher engagement. For example, a major quick-service restaurant chain ran an interactive CTV campaign that displayed a QR code with a localized offer based on the viewer’s ZIP code. The campaign achieved a 4x higher redemption rate compared to the brand’s standard digital coupon distribution. The combination of location-based content and interactive advertising created a direct path from TV screen to in-store purchase. Location-Based Personalization Location data enables some of the most practical applications of CTV personalization. Brands can tailor messaging based on proximity to retail locations, regional product availability, local events, or even weather conditions. A home improvement retailer served ads promoting snow removal equipment in northern markets and patio furniture in southern markets during the same national campaign window. A beverage brand adjusted its creative to feature cold drinks during heat waves and warm beverages during cold snaps, using real-time weather API integrations. A tourism board targeted viewers within a three-hour driving radius with weekend getaway promotions, achieving a 28% lift in website traffic from those regions. Perion has supported similar location-aware CTV campaigns through its advertising platform, enabling brands to activate geographic targeting alongside creative personalization to deliver locally relevant messages at scale. Key Platforms and Tools for Your Personalization Strategy Building a CTV creative personalization strategy requires selecting the right combination of demand-side platforms, creative management tools, data providers, and measurement partners. The technology ecosystem has matured significantly, offering advertisers multiple options at each layer of the stack. Technology Stack Components Layer Function Example Providers Demand-Side Platform (DSP) Programmatic buying and audience targeting The Trade Desk, DV360, Perion Creative Management Platform Dynamic creative assembly and versioning Innovid, Flashtalking (Mediaocean), Celtra Data Management Audience segmentation and identity resolution LiveRamp, TransUnion, Experian Measurement and Attribution Campaign performance and incrementality testing iSpot.tv, Samba TV, TVSquared (Innovid) CTV Inventory Supply Access to streaming ad inventory Roku, Samsung Ads, LG Ad Solutions, Hulu Choosing the Right Partners Not all platforms support the same depth of personalization. When evaluating partners, consider the following criteria: Creative flexibility: Can the platform support video-level dynamic assembly, or is personalization limited to companion banners and overlays? Data integration: Does the platform accept first-party data uploads, and does it support clean room environments for privacy-safe matching? Scale of inventory: Can the platform reach your target audience across multiple streaming services and device types? Reporting granularity: Does the platform provide creative-level performance data broken down by audience segment? Perion’s CTV offering is notable for combining demand-side buying capabilities with built-in creative optimization tools, reducing the need for advertisers to stitch together multiple point solutions. This integrated approach simplifies campaign management while maintaining the flexibility needed for sophisticated personalization strategies. Common Challenges in CTV Personalization and How to Solve Them Despite its potential, CTV creative personalization comes with real obstacles. Understanding these challenges upfront helps advertisers plan more effectively and avoid costly missteps. Challenge 1: Fragmented Identity Across Devices CTV devices are typically shared by multiple household members, making it difficult to target a specific individual. Unlike mobile phones, a Roku or Fire TV Stick does not belong to a single user. Solution: Focus on household-level targeting rather than individual targeting. Use probabilistic models to infer the most likely viewer based on time of day, content genre, and viewing patterns. Partner with identity providers that specialize in CTV household graphs. Challenge 2: Limited Creative Production Resources Producing multiple video ad variations is expensive and time-consuming. Many brands struggle to create enough creative assets to support true personalization. Solution: Adopt modular creative frameworks where a single base video can be customized through swappable end cards, text overlays, voiceover variations, and product inserts. DCO platforms reduce the production burden significantly. Challenge 3: Inconsistent Measurement Standards CTV lacks a unified measurement standard comparable to digital display’s click-through rate. Different platforms report different metrics, making cross-platform comparison difficult. Solution: Establish a consistent measurement framework before launching campaigns. Define primary KPIs such as completed view rate, brand lift, website visit rate, and incremental reach. Use third-party measurement partners to provide a neutral view of performance. Challenge 4: Frequency Management Without reliable cross-platform identity, the same viewer may see the same ad too many times across different streaming apps, leading to fatigue and negative brand perception. Solution: Work with DSPs and supply-side platforms that support frequency capping at the household or device level. Perion and other platforms offer cross-publisher frequency management to reduce over-exposure while maintaining reach goals. Measuring the ROI of Your Personalized CTV Campaigns Proving the return on investment of CTV creative personalization requires a measurement approach that goes beyond basic video completion rates. Advertisers need to connect CTV exposure to downstream business outcomes. Key Metrics to Track Incremental reach: How many unique households did the CTV campaign reach that were not exposed through linear TV or other channels? Brand lift: Did ad awareness, brand consideration, or purchase intent increase among exposed audiences compared to a control group? Website and app visitation: Did viewers visit the advertiser’s website or app within a defined window after CTV ad exposure? Conversion attribution: Can specific purchases or sign-ups be attributed to CTV impressions through deterministic or probabilistic matching? Creative performance variance: Which personalized creative versions drove the strongest results across different audience segments? Attribution Models for CTV CTV attribution is more complex than standard digital attribution because viewers typically do not click directly from a TV ad. Instead, advertisers rely on methods such as: Exposed vs. control analysis: Comparing outcomes between households exposed to the CTV ad and a matched control group that was not. Multi-touch attribution (MTA): Assigning fractional credit to CTV alongside other touchpoints in the customer journey. Marketing mix modeling (MMM): Using statistical models to estimate CTV’s contribution to overall sales alongside other media channels. The most rigorous approach combines multiple methods. For instance, an advertiser might use exposed-control testing to validate brand lift, MTA to understand CTV’s role in the conversion path, and MMM to assess long-term sales impact. This layered measurement strategy provides confidence that personalized CTV campaigns are delivering genuine business value. Perion provides campaign analytics that include creative-level performance breakdowns, helping advertisers identify which personalized variations are driving the strongest ROI and reallocate budgets accordingly. What’s Next: The Future of CTV Creative Personalization in 2026 CTV creative personalization is maturing rapidly, and several trends will shape its trajectory through 2026 and beyond. Advertisers who understand these shifts can position themselves to capture outsized value from the channel. Trend 1: AI-Powered Creative Generation Generative AI tools are beginning to assist with video production, enabling faster creation of personalized ad variations. While fully AI-generated TV commercials remain uncommon, AI is already accelerating tasks like script variation, voiceover production, and background scene generation. This will lower the cost barrier to producing large volumes of personalized creative assets. Trend 2: Shoppable CTV Experiences Interactive advertising on CTV is moving toward direct commerce. Viewers will increasingly be able to purchase products directly from the TV screen using remote-based navigation or by scanning QR codes with their phones. This collapses the gap between ad exposure and conversion, making CTV a true performance channel. Trend 3: Clean Room-Based Collaboration Data clean rooms are enabling advertisers and publishers to share audience insights without exposing raw personal data. This technology will expand the scope of CTV personalization by allowing brands to match their first-party data against publisher viewing data in a privacy-compliant environment. The result is more precise targeting without increased privacy risk. Trend 4: Cross-Screen Creative Sequencing Rather than treating CTV as an isolated channel, forward-thinking advertisers are building creative sequences that span CTV, mobile, and desktop. A viewer might see a brand awareness spot on CTV, followed by a product-specific ad on their phone the next day, and a retargeting offer on desktop later that week. This orchestrated approach requires unified identity and creative management, areas where platforms like Perion are investing heavily. The direction is clear: CTV creative personalization will become more automated, more interactive, and more tightly integrated with the broader digital advertising ecosystem. Brands that invest in the right data infrastructure, creative workflows, and measurement capabilities now will be best positioned to capitalize on these advances as they become standard practice. title: Qventus Care Gap and Coding Automation Suite Increases Malnutrition Code Capture by 57% as the Suite Expands to Pressure Injuries
summary: In the months since launch, the Malnutrition Care Automation captures $17.1M in additional annualized reimbursement across clients and reduces length of stay by up 2.5 days San Francisco, CA (August…
body_text: In the months since launch, the Malnutrition Care Automation captures $17.1M in additional annualized reimbursement across clients and reduces length of stay by up 2.5 days San Francisco, CA (August 11, 2026) — Qventus , the leader in automated care operations, today announces that health systems using its Care Gap and Coding Automation Suite have captured $17.1M in additional annualized reimbursement with the Malnutrition Care Automation, with one client seeing $7.6M in annualized reimbursement in the first four months. The company also announced the latest automation that identifies patients at risk of developing pressure injuries and automatically orchestrates the appropriate interventions and accurate coding. The speed to ROI and launch of the second solution in the Care Gap and Coding Suite showcase the velocity of product advancements built on Qventus’ AI Platform. The Suite empowers health systems to expand into new use cases and care settings without another vendor, integration, or implementation cycle. Qventus shifts left to improve clinical and quality outcomes, captures $17.1M in annualized reimbursement Qventus launched the Care Gap and Coding Automation Suite in February as a system of action embedded in existing EHR workflows to identify missed diagnoses, orchestrate timely clinical interventions, and complete documentation in real time. The suite shifts clinical interventions left, surfacing conditions the moment the patient is admitted and taking action, rather than a delayed retrospective audit after discharge. The first automation in the suite, Malnutrition Care Automation, uses chart mining to identify malnourished patients, pre-populates the nutrition consult order, surfaces key insights to dietitians to aid in assessment, and prompts diagnosis documentation for MCC/CC capture before the coding window closes. “At Jackson Health System, we’re committed to delivering exceptional, evidence-based care for every patient we serve, including many with complex medical needs. By leveraging the Malnutrition Care Automation solution, we’re identifying at-risk patients earlier than traditional screening methods alone, allowing our caregivers to intervene sooner and improve outcomes,” said Monica Puga, Chief Transformation Officer, Jackson Health System. “Our partnership with Qventus, coupled with its AI-assisted capabilities, has allowed us to quickly extend this capability across our clinical operations, supporting our mission to deliver the right care at the right time for the patients that depend on us.” Qventus honors its commitment to delivering measurable ROI to its clients Since launch, health systems have reported over a $17M lift in annualized reimbursement revenue, and reported the following results: Jackson Health System saw 57% increase in code capture, realizing a 3.3x annualized ROI. A midwestern AMC reported a 15% lift in code capture and an improvement in mortality O:E. An Ohio-based nonprofit health system reduced time to nutrition care for malnourished patients by 2.5 days. A Wisconsin-based non-profit health system reports that patients coded for malnutrition are experiencing a 0.6-day reduction in length of stay – the equivalent of 220 annualized days saved. A Midwestern health system achieved a 14% increase in code capture at one of its hospitals. “Providers are trained to treat the acute problem first. Conditions like malnutrition and pressure injuries get treated late or not at all, and the patient goes home sicker than they needed to,” said Jason Cohen, MD, Chief Medical Officer for Inpatient, Qventus. “This suite moves recognition and intervention to the front of the stay, when treating the condition can still shorten length of stay and lower readmission risk. It also means providers aren’t spending time answering CDI queries about that patient a week later, when they are already caring for someone else. We’ve seen that proven out by our clients that are reporting decreased LOS and provider time saved after only weeks of deploying the Care Gap and Coding Suite.” Second solution in the Suite closes the gap for pressure injury care Qventus launched the second solution in the Care Gap and Coding Suite to identify patients at risk for pressure injuries. Embedded in existing EHR workflows, it continuously analyzes patient data to identify patients at elevated risk of having or developing a pressure injury and orchestrates the next clinical action, including initiating prevention order sets, recommending support surfaces, prompting timely skin assessments, and confirming that repositioning interventions are completed. Documentation follows the same path, capturing skin assessment findings, present-on-admission status, prevention activities, and pressure injury staging as care is delivered rather than after discharge. Present-on-admission accuracy carries particular weight for pressure injuries. An injury documented during the admission window is recorded as present on admission; the same injury captured later is counted as hospital-acquired, which affects performance under the CMS Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program. With Qventus, health systems reduce preventable hospital-acquired pressure injuries, improve quality performance, and avoid an average treatment cost of more than $22,000 per hospital-acquired pressure injury. “Automated care operations have become critical infrastructure in the tech stack as health systems consolidate around a single AI platform. That investment pays off and compounds when the next solution can be quickly turned on to generate guaranteed ROI at scale,” said Mudit Garg, Co-founder and CEO, Qventus. “We went from launching the Care Gap and Coding Automation Suite to a second live solution in a matter of months, with strong returns for health systems. That pace comes from a decade of building and refining the Qventus AI Platform, and it is what our clients are counting on when they expand with us across the enterprise.” About Qventus Qventus uses AI to intelligently automate operations across care settings to help health systems secure the margins needed to achieve their mission of delivering exceptional care to patients in their communities. Leveraged by more than 150 hospital facilities, Qventus’ enterprise platform and AI solution suite reduce the administrative burden, identify potential issues upstream, surface suggested interventions, and actually take action to solve problems for busy healthcare staff—a collective system of action that sits on top of a hospital’s enterprise systems of record. Qventus unlocks best-in-industry ROI by driving strategic surgical growth, creating capacity, and reducing costs, all while delivering powerful insights to help solve long standing operational challenges once and for all. 100% of clients say they consider Qventus part of their long term strategy.

body_text: Delivers Total Revenues of $3.8 Billion, Representing 5% Reported Growth Compared to Second Quarter 2025 and a U.S. GAAP Net Loss of $119 Million Total Revenues Were Up 3.5% Operationally Compared to Second Quarter 2025 Adjusted EBITDA was $1.2 Billion, Up 8% Operationally Compared to Second Quarter 2025 Advances Key Pipeline Milestones, Including U.S. FDA Approval of Gwyn LoTM Announces Sale of Global Rights to Tyrvaya® Returns Approximately $550 Million of Capital to Shareholders, Including Through Share Repurchases; Reduces Gross Leverage Ratio to 2.9x Raises 2026 Financial Guidance Midpoints for All Metrics [1] PITTSBURGH , Aug. 6, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Viatris Inc . (Nasdaq: VTRS), a global healthcare company, today announced its second-quarter 2026 financial results. Executive Commentary "Our second-quarter results reflect another quarter of strong execution and reinforce the momentum we're building across our business," said Scott A. Smith , CEO, Viatris . "Commercial execution, pipeline progress and the early benefits of our enterprise-wide strategic review continue strengthening our business and improving our financial performance. Our strong first-half results give us the confidence to raise our full-year guidance. We expect a more balanced operating environment in the second half of the year and we remain focused on disciplined execution, investing behind our future growth drivers and creating long-term value for patients and shareholders." "We delivered another strong quarter of Total Revenues and Adjusted EBITDA growth over the prior year, reflecting continued strong operational execution," said Paul Campbell , Interim CFO , Chief Accounting Officer & Corporate Controller, Viatris . "At the same time, we continued to execute on our balanced capital allocation strategy, returning approximately $550 million to shareholders, including approximately $270 million of share repurchases occurring through early August. Financial Highlights for the Second Quarter of 2026 Total revenues were $3.8 billion, up 5% on a reported basis and up 3.5% on an operational basis compared to second-quarter 2025 results, primarily driven by new product sales in Developed Markets and strong growth in Greater China. Brands net sales reflect continued strength in Greater China and Emerging Markets. Generics net sales reflect contributions from new product launches, in addition to growth in certain products in Developed Markets, partially offset by supply constraints in the ARV business within Emerging Markets. The Company generated approximately $101 million in new product revenues (approximately $172 million for the year) and continues expecting to deliver approximately $450 million to $550 million in new product revenues in full-year 2026. U.S. GAAP net loss was $119 million compared to U.S. GAAP net loss of $5 million in the second quarter of 2025 and U.S. GAAP diluted loss per share was $(0.10) compared to a loss of less than $(0.01) per share in the second quarter of 2025. The loss in the second quarter of 2026 was primarily driven by a non-cash charge of $177.8 million related to the planned sale of the product rights for Tyrvaya® and the write down of that intangible asset to fair value, less cost to sell. Adjusted EBITDA was $1.2 billion, up 10% on a reported basis and up 8% on an operational basis compared to the second quarter of 2025, and adjusted EPS was $0.69 per share, up 11% on a reported basis and up 9% on an operational basis compared to the second quarter of 2025. The Company generated U.S. GAAP net cash provided by operating activities of $382 million ($770 million for the year) and free cash flow, excluding the impact of transaction-related and restructuring-related costs, of $449 million ($908 million for the year). Additional Highlights In August, the Company signed a definitive agreement to sell the global product rights for Tyrvaya to Harrow, Inc., a leading provider of ophthalmic disease management solutions in North America, for an upfront payment of $30 million and an additional $70 million in commercial contingent milestone payments. The transaction reflects the Company's continued focus on prioritizing its capital, talent and resources toward opportunities it believes offer the greatest long-term growth potential. In July, the Company announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Gwyn LoTM (norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol transdermal system), a new combined hormonal contraceptive patch with low-dose estrogen. The Company expects Gwyn Lo to be commercially available later this year. In July, the Company completed the sale of its equity position in Biocon Limited for a pre-tax total consideration of approximately $380 million. The pre-tax sale proceeds include the impacts of an approximate 2.7% block sale discount to market, transaction fees and the strengthening of the U.S. dollar since the Company obtained the equity in January 2026. This sale completes the Company's monetization of its stake in Biocon Biologics Limited for a total of approximately $780 million. In June, the FDA approved the Company's generic ferric carboxymaltose injection in three strengths: 750 mg/15 mL, 1000 mg/20 mL and 100 mg/2 mL. Ferric carboxymaltose is a substitutable generic version of Injectafer®, which is indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anemia and non-dialysis dependent chronic kidney disease, and iron deficiency. In June, the Company announced positive top-line results from a Phase 3 clinical trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of VR-205 (targeted-release budesonide formulation) (Nefecon®) in Japanese adult patients with primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy at risk of developing end-stage renal disease. In May, the FDA inspected the Company's oral solid dose manufacturing facility in Nashik, India, and issued Form 483 observations. The Company responded to the Form 483 observations and promptly initiated a comprehensive remediation plan. The Company has also engaged independent third-party subject matter experts to support its remediation plan. Activities under the remediation plan are ongoing and have led to intermittent disruptions at the facility. While production at the facility has resumed, the temporary manufacturing suspension due to the fire at the facility in February along with these intermittent disruptions are expected to impact product supply in the second half of the year. The Company currently anticipates the impact of product supply disruptions to be between $100 million and $150 million to total revenues in the second half of 2026. In May, the Company announced that the FDA accepted for review the New Drug Application for MR-107A-02 (fast-acting meloxicam), a non-opioid, for the treatment of moderate-to-severe acute pain. The FDA has assigned a PDUFA goal date of December 27, 2026. The Company signed a distribution agreement with Accord Healthcare to commercialize three biosimilar products (filgrastim, ustekinumab, teriparatide) in France. In addition, the Company signed a co-promotion partnership with Idorsia Ltd. for Quvivq® in Italy and Canada. These transactions reflect the Company's disciplined business development strategy of expanding its portfolio through complementary, accretive products that leverage its regional capabilities and commercial strengths. Capital Allocation Through August 5, 2026, the Company has returned approximately $550 million of capital to shareholders, including approximately $270 million through share repurchases at a weighted average purchase price of $16.42 per share. The Company has approximately $730 million remaining under its existing board-authorized share repurchase program, providing continued flexibility to return additional capital to shareholders. The Company repaid approximately $900 million of debt that matured in June 2026, refinancing the remaining balance with a public offering of €650 million aggregate principal amount of 4.250% euro-denominated senior notes due 2033. As a result, the Company ended the quarter with a gross leverage ratio of 2.9x. 2026 Financial Guidance Viatris is raising the midpoints of its 2026 financial guidance ranges, each as set forth below. Non-GAAP Financial Measures This press release includes the presentation and discussion of certain financial information that differs from what is reported under accounting principles generally accepted in the United States ("U.S. GAAP"). These non-GAAP financial measures, including, but not limited to, adjusted gross profit, adjusted gross margins, adjusted net earnings, adjusted EPS, EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, free cash flow, free cash flow excluding the impact of transaction-related and restructuring-related costs, adjusted R&D and as a % of total revenues, adjusted SG&A and as a % of total revenues, adjusted earnings from operations, adjusted interest expense, adjusted other income, net, adjusted effective tax rate, constant currency total revenues, constant currency net sales, constant currency adjusted EBITDA, constant currency adjusted EPS, notional debt, gross leverage ratio and long-term gross leverage ratio target, are presented in order to supplement investors' and other readers' understanding and assessment of the financial performance of Viatris Inc. ("Viatris" or the "Company"). Free cash flow refers to U.S. GAAP net cash provided by operating activities less capital expenditures. Management uses these measures internally for forecasting, budgeting, measuring its operating performance, and incentive-based awards. Primarily due to acquisitions, divestitures and other significant events which may impact comparability of our periodic operating results, Viatris believes that an evaluation of its ongoing operations (and comparisons of its current operations with historical and future operations) would be difficult if the disclosure of its financial results was limited to financial measures prepared only in accordance with U.S. GAAP. We believe that non-GAAP financial measures are useful supplemental information for our investors and when considered together with our U.S. GAAP financial measures and the reconciliation to the most directly comparable U.S. GAAP financial measure, provide a more complete understanding of the factors and trends affecting our operations. The financial performance of the Company is measured by senior management, in part, using adjusted metrics included herein, along with other performance metrics. In addition, the Company believes that including EBITDA and supplemental adjustments applied in presenting adjusted EBITDA is appropriate to provide additional information to investors to demonstrate the Company's ability to comply with financial debt covenants and assess the Company's ability to incur additional indebtedness. The Company also believes that adjusted EBITDA better focuses management on the Company's underlying operational results and true business performance and is used, in part, for management's incentive compensation. We also report sales performance using the non-GAAP financial measures of "constant currency", also referred to herein as "operational change", total revenues, net sales, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS. These measures provide information on the change in total revenues, net sales, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS assuming that foreign currency exchange rates had not changed between the prior and current period. The comparisons presented at constant currency rates reflect comparative local currency sales at the prior year's foreign exchange rates. We routinely evaluate our net sales, total revenues, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS performance at constant currency so that sales results can be viewed without the impact of foreign currency exchange rates, thereby facilitating a period-to-period comparison of our operational activities and believe that this presentation also provides useful information to investors for the same reason. Philadelphia Medicaid Fraud Case: 19 Defendants Charged in Alleged $4 Million Healthcare Scheme
summary: Federal Authorities Launch Major Investigation Into Alleged Pennsylvania Medicaid Fraud A major healthcare fraud investigation in Philadelphia has resulted in charges against 19 individuals accused of participating in an alleged scheme involving more than $4 million in Pennsylvania Medicaid funds. Federal and state officials announced the charges as part of a wider effort to protect government healthcare programs and prevent financial abuse targeting services designed for vulnerable communities
body_text: Federal Authorities Launch Major Investigation Into Alleged Pennsylvania Medicaid Fraud A major healthcare fraud investigation in Philadelphia has resulted in charges against 19 individuals accused of participating in an alleged scheme involving more than $4 million in Pennsylvania Medicaid funds. Federal and state officials announced the charges as part of a wider effort to protect government healthcare programs and prevent financial abuse targeting services designed for vulnerable communities. The case focuses on allegations involving home healthcare services, a sector that provides essential support for elderly individuals and people who need assistance with daily activities while remaining in their own homes. Authorities stated that the alleged fraud involved healthcare workers, Medicaid recipients, and individuals connected to a home healthcare agency. Officials emphasized that Medicaid programs exist to provide necessary care for people who depend on government assistance. When fraudulent claims are submitted, resources intended for patients and families can be diverted away from those who genuinely need support. Details of the Alleged Philadelphia Healthcare Fraud Operation According to officials, 19 defendants have been charged in connection with the alleged scheme. Eighteen of those individuals were charged during a coordinated law enforcement operation involving federal and state agencies working together to investigate suspected healthcare fraud. Authorities said the defendants include home health aides, Medicaid beneficiaries, and owners connected to a home healthcare organization allegedly involved in improper billing activities. Some individuals charged in the case reportedly have previous criminal histories, though all defendants are entitled to a fair legal process and are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. The investigation was led by agencies focused on identifying fraud within government healthcare systems. Officials described the operation as part of a larger national effort to uncover illegal activities that impact Medicare and Medicaid programs. Pennsylvania has one of the largest home healthcare spending programs in the country. Officials noted that the state spent more than $8 billion on home care services in 2025, making oversight and accountability especially important. Government Officials Highlight Need for Stronger Fraud Prevention During a press conference announcing the charges, officials discussed concerns about the challenges of detecting fraudulent healthcare claims. They explained that some billing patterns can make it difficult for agencies to determine whether services are medically necessary or accurately reported. Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, raised concerns about personal care claims in Pennsylvania that frequently use broad diagnostic descriptions. According to officials, a high percentage of claims were submitted under categories such as "illness unspecified," which may limit the ability of regulators to properly review services. Federal officials stated that improved data collection, stronger monitoring systems, and increased cooperation between agencies are important tools in identifying suspicious activity. The goal of these enforcement actions is not only to prosecute alleged offenders but also to strengthen healthcare programs so that taxpayer-funded resources reach qualified patients. Expansion of Healthcare Fraud Enforcement Efforts The Philadelphia case comes as federal authorities continue expanding healthcare fraud investigations across the United States. The Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division announced an expansion of its Northeast Health Care Fraud Strike Force to include Philadelphia. The expanded operation will work with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania to investigate and prosecute healthcare fraud cases in the region. National healthcare fraud investigations have resulted in thousands of prosecutions involving billions of dollars in alleged improper payments. Officials said these efforts are designed to protect federal healthcare programs, insurance systems, and patients who rely on medical assistance. Healthcare fraud can take many forms, including false billing, unnecessary services, identity misuse, and misrepresentation of medical conditions. Authorities continue to encourage stronger oversight throughout the healthcare industry to reduce financial losses and protect beneficiaries. Why Medicaid Fraud Investigations Matter Medicaid is a critical program that helps millions of Americans access healthcare services. Funding is used for medical care, personal assistance, nursing support, and other essential services. When fraudulent claims are made, the impact can extend beyond financial losses. Fraud can reduce available resources, increase administrative costs, and create challenges for legitimate healthcare providers and patients. Home healthcare services are particularly important because they allow many elderly and disabled individuals to receive assistance without leaving their homes. Officials stressed that protecting these programs helps ensure patients receive safe and reliable care. Law enforcement agencies say they will continue targeting individuals and organizations suspected of abusing healthcare systems while working to improve fraud detection methods. Broader Healthcare Fraud Crackdown Across the Nation During the same announcement, officials also discussed other healthcare enforcement actions, including efforts involving Medicare providers in California. Authorities reported that numerous hospice providers had been removed from the Medicare program following investigations and reviews. Officials said these actions demonstrate a broader commitment to preventing fraudulent organizations from accessing taxpayer-funded healthcare programs. The government’s increased focus on healthcare fraud reflects growing concerns about protecting public funds while maintaining access to quality care for eligible beneficiaries. What Happens Next in the Philadelphia Case The 19 defendants charged in the Philadelphia Medicaid fraud investigation will face the legal process as the case moves forward. Prosecutors must present evidence in court, while defendants have the right to defend themselves against the allegations. Healthcare fraud cases often involve detailed financial records, billing documents, patient information, and testimony from investigators and healthcare professionals. The outcome of this case will depend on the evidence presented through the judicial system. Officials said the investigation represents one part of a continuing effort to identify and stop fraudulent activity within healthcare programs. Conclusion The Philadelphia Medicaid fraud case highlights the ongoing challenges faced by government healthcare programs in preventing financial abuse. With millions of dollars allegedly involved, authorities are increasing enforcement efforts to protect Medicaid funding and ensure assistance reaches people who need it most. As investigations continue, officials say collaboration between federal agencies, state authorities, healthcare providers, and communities remains essential in reducing fraud and improving accountability across the healthcare system. Source NTD Television, August 4, 2026. Disclaimer The information in this article is based on publicly reported allegations and official statements. The individuals mentioned in connection with the case are accused of wrongdoing but are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in a court of law. This article is intended for informational purposes only and does not represent a legal judgment or final determination of guilt.

title: Are Marketing Agencies Going to Die?
summary: Short answer: no. But the agencies that survive will look nothing like the agencies that exist today.
body_text: Short answer: no. But the agencies that survive will look nothing like the agencies that exist today. The AI anxiety in the agency world is real. When a founder can generate ad copy with Claude, build landing pages with AI-assisted tools, and set up basic automation without a dedicated ops person — the obvious question is: what do I need an agency for? It's the right question. And the answer is more nuanced than either "agencies are dead" or "agencies will be fine." What's actually being disrupted AI isn't replacing agencies. It's replacing the commodity services that many agencies have built their revenue on. Service Status Why Ad copy and creative Commoditizing fast AI generates decent first drafts. The gap between AI-generated and agency-generated copy is shrinking monthly. Basic landing pages Commoditizing Template-based builders + AI content = good-enough landing pages without agency involvement. Email sequence writing Commoditizing AI writes solid nurture emails. The strategy behind them still requires expertise, but the execution doesn't require an agency. Social media management Partially commoditizing Scheduling and basic content creation are automatable. Community management and brand voice still need humans. Reporting and dashboards Commoditizing AI can pull data, build dashboards, and summarize performance. The insight extraction still needs a strategist, but the assembly doesn't. Campaign strategy Not yet AI can suggest tactics but can't evaluate market position, competitive dynamics, or business context the way an experienced strategist can. Lead ops and conversion optimization Not at all This requires understanding a client's specific sales process, CRM architecture, routing logic, and funnel mechanics. AI tools help but can't replace the diagnosis and implementation. The agencies most at risk are the ones selling execution — the deliverables (copy, pages, emails) that AI can now produce at 80% quality for 10% of the cost. The agencies least at risk are the ones selling outcomes — strategy, implementation, and measurable improvement in metrics that matter. The new agency model The agencies that thrive will shift from selling hours and deliverables to selling results and infrastructure. From content production to conversion engineering. Instead of "we'll write your blog posts and emails," the value proposition becomes "we'll fix your lead flow so 30% more of your leads become meetings." The output isn't content — it's a measurable improvement in a business metric. From campaign management to systems architecture. Instead of managing ad campaigns and reporting on impressions, agencies build and optimize the infrastructure between the ad click and the sales conversation. Capture, qualification, routing, and response — the layer most companies can't build themselves and AI tools can't configure automatically. From retainer-based to outcome-based. When the deliverable is "more meetings" or "lower cost per meeting," pricing can be tied to outcomes instead of hours. This is harder to scope but more defensible — because the client pays for results, not time. Why lead ops is the agency opportunity Most B2B companies between $5M and $50M in revenue don't have the internal ops resources to build a proper lead operations system. They have a marketing team running campaigns, a sales team working leads, and a gap between them filled with duct tape. Agencies that can diagnose and fix that gap — using tools like Surface to implement capture, qualification, routing, and instant response — deliver immediate, measurable value that AI can't replicate. The diagnosis requires understanding the client's specific business. The implementation requires configuring systems to match their sales structure. The optimization requires ongoing analysis of conversion data. This is consultative, technical, high-value work. It's the opposite of commodity content production. And it's the kind of work that makes clients stay for years, not months. [IMAGE: A simple before/after. Left side: "Old agency model" — Content production, Campaign management, Monthly reporting, Retainer-based. Right side: "New agency model" — Conversion engineering, Systems architecture, Real-time metrics, Outcome-based. White background, blue ( #4F6DF5 ) accent, flat design.] Where Surface fits Surface gives agencies a platform to deliver lead ops as a service. Instead of recommending that clients fix their own capture and routing, agencies can implement Surface across their client portfolio — configuring qualification, routing, and response for each client's specific sales process. For agencies looking to move upmarket from commodity services, lead ops infrastructure is the highest-value, most defensible offering available. Surface is the tool that makes it deliverable.

title: Cómo causar una factura con IVA y retenciones aplicadas
summary: Causar una factura con IVA y retenciones aplicadas significa registrar en un solo asiento contable tres movimientos distintos: el ingreso o el costo/gasto por el valor neto de la operación, el IVA generado o descontable, y las retenciones.
body_text: Causar una factura con IVA y retenciones aplicadas significa registrar en un solo asiento contable tres movimientos distintos: el ingreso o el costo/gasto por el valor neto de la operación, el IVA generado o descontable, y las retenciones (renta, IVA o ICA) que el comprador practica al vendedor o que la empresa debe practicar como agente retenedor. Cada retención tiene una base de cálculo distinta y afecta cuentas diferentes según si la empresa está vendiendo o comprando. A continuación se explica el proceso completo, con tarifas y bases vigentes para 2026. Qué es una factura con IVA y retenciones aplicadas Cuando una empresa vende un bien o presta un servicio gravado con IVA a un cliente que es agente de retención, la factura resultante puede combinar hasta tres impuestos distintos sobre una misma operación: el IVA generado por la venta, la retención en la fuente a título de renta que el cliente le practica al vendedor, y —en algunos casos— la retención en la fuente a título de IVA (reteIVA) y la retención de industria y comercio (reteICA). Cada uno de estos conceptos tiene una base de cálculo diferente y un tratamiento contable propio, por lo que causar correctamente la factura exige separar cada componente en la cuenta que le corresponde. Los tres tipos de retención que pueden aparecer en una factura Retención en la fuente a título de renta (retefuente): es un anticipo del impuesto de renta que el comprador descuenta al vendedor y consigna a la DIAN a nombre de este. Se calcula sobre el valor de la operación antes de IVA. Retención en la fuente a título de IVA (reteIVA): es un anticipo del IVA que el comprador descuenta al vendedor cuando actúa como agente de retención de IVA. Se calcula sobre el valor del IVA generado en la factura, no sobre el valor total de la operación. Retención de industria y comercio (reteICA): es un anticipo del impuesto municipal de industria y comercio, cuya tarifa y base la fija cada municipio o distrito dentro de los rangos que autoriza la ley, por lo que puede variar según dónde se realice la operación. Cómo se calculan el IVA y las retenciones sobre una misma factura El orden de cálculo es clave para no cometer errores: primero se determina la base gravable de la operación (el valor antes de impuestos), luego se calcula el IVA sobre esa base, y finalmente se calculan las retenciones. La retefuente y la reteICA se calculan sobre la base gravable sin IVA; la reteIVA se calcula sobre el valor del IVA ya liquidado, no sobre el total de la factura ni sobre la base gravable. Un error frecuente es aplicar la retención en la fuente sobre el valor total de la factura (base más IVA), lo que genera una retención más alta de la que corresponde legalmente. Bases y tarifas de retención en la fuente vigentes en 2026 Desde el 1 de julio de 2026, tras la reactivación de las bases mínimas del Decreto 572 de 2025 por decisión del Consejo de Estado, estas son las cifras que deben usarse: Concepto Base mínima 2026 (UVT / pesos) Tarifa declarante Tarifa no declarante Compras generales 10 UVT ($523.740) 2,5 % 3,5 % Servicios generales 2 UVT ($104.748) 4 % 6 % Honorarios y comisiones (persona jurídica) Sin cuantía mínima 11 % — Honorarios y comisiones (persona natural) Sin cuantía mínima 11 % o 10 %, según el caso 10 % Arrendamiento de bienes inmuebles 10 UVT ($523.740) 3,5 % 3,5 % Arrendamiento de bienes muebles Sin cuantía mínima 4 % 4 % Compras agrícolas o pecuarias sin procesar 92 UVT 1,5 % 1,5 % La UVT vigente para el año gravable 2026 es de $52.374, fijada por la Resolución DIAN 000238 de 2025. Los porcentajes de honorarios varían según si la persona natural suscribió o no más de un contrato en el año, o si sus ingresos superan cierto monto; conviene validar el caso concreto antes de aplicar la tarifa. Para la reteIVA, la tarifa general es del 15 % del valor del IVA generado en la factura, y sube al 100 % en operaciones especiales como pagos a personas sin residencia en el país por servicios digitales o electrónicos, o compra de chatarra y tabaco a proveedores específicos. La reteICA depende del acuerdo municipal aplicable en cada jurisdicción, por lo que su tarifa debe consultarse directamente en la administración tributaria local. Causación desde la perspectiva del vendedor: las retenciones que te aplican Cuando la empresa emite la factura de venta y el cliente le practica retenciones, esos valores no se pierden: se registran como un activo (anticipo de impuestos) que la empresa podrá descontar en sus declaraciones de renta e IVA. Es decir, en la venta las retenciones son un derecho a favor de quien factura, no un gasto. Causación desde la perspectiva del comprador: las retenciones que tú practicas Cuando la empresa recibe la factura de un proveedor y actúa como agente de retención, debe descontar el valor correspondiente del pago al proveedor y registrar un pasivo a favor de la DIAN por cada tipo de retención practicada, que se cancelará al presentar la declaración mensual de retención en la fuente (formulario 350). Cuentas PUC más usadas para causar facturas con IVA y retenciones Código PUC Nombre de la cuenta Uso 1305 Clientes nacionales Cuenta por cobrar en la venta 135515 Anticipo de retención en la fuente por cobrar Cuando el cliente te practica retefuente en una venta 135517 Anticipo de reteIVA por cobrar Cuando el cliente te practica reteIVA en una venta 135518 Anticipo de reteICA por cobrar Cuando el cliente te practica reteICA en una venta 2408 IVA generado (venta) o IVA descontable (compra) Según el rol en la operación 236505 Retención en la fuente por pagar Cuando tú practicas retefuente en una compra 236801 Retención de IVA por pagar (reteIVA) Cuando tú practicas reteIVA en una compra 236715 Retención de ICA por pagar Cuando tú practicas reteICA en una compra 2205 Proveedores nacionales Cuenta por pagar en la compra Ejemplo de causación: factura de venta de servicios con retefuente, reteIVA y reteICA Una empresa presta un servicio profesional por $5.000.000 más IVA del 19 %. El cliente es agente de retención y aplica retención en la fuente por honorarios del 11 %, reteIVA del 15 % sobre el IVA generado y reteICA del 0,7 % sobre la base gravable. Cuenta Débito Crédito 1305 Clientes nacionales 5.257.500 135515 Anticipo de retención en la fuente por cobrar (11 % de $5.000.000) 550.000 135517 Anticipo de reteIVA por cobrar (15 % de $950.000) 142.500 135518 Anticipo de reteICA por cobrar (0,7 % de $5.000.000) 35.000 4115 Ingresos por servicios 5.000.000 2408 IVA generado (19 % de $5.000.000) 950.000 Total débitos: $5.985.000; total créditos: $5.950.000; la diferencia corresponde a que la reteICA se descuenta del pago pero no reduce el valor de la factura ante la DIAN, sino que se resta directamente del efectivo que recibirá la empresa. Al conciliar el pago, el valor neto que efectivamente ingresará a bancos será $5.950.000 menos la suma de las tres retenciones ($727.500), es decir, $5.222.500. Ejemplo de causación: factura de compra de servicios con retenciones practicadas La misma operación, vista desde el comprador que recibe el servicio y actúa como agente de retención. Cuenta Débito Crédito 5135 / 6135 Gastos o costos por servicios 5.000.000 2408 IVA descontable (19 % de $5.000.000) 950.000 236505 Retención en la fuente por pagar 550.000 236801 Retención de IVA por pagar 142.500 236715 Retención de ICA por pagar 35.000 2205 Proveedores nacionales 5.222.500 Aquí el pasivo con el proveedor (2205) ya refleja el valor neto que efectivamente se le pagará, una vez descontadas las tres retenciones practicadas. Casos especiales al causar facturas con IVA y retenciones Operaciones con no responsables de IVA: si el proveedor no es responsable de IVA, la factura no genera IVA descontable ni reteIVA, pero sí puede generar retefuente y reteICA según el concepto. Servicios prestados por personas no residentes: la reteIVA sube al 100 % del IVA generado, ya que el prestador extranjero no puede ser fiscalizado directamente por la DIAN. Autorretención: algunas empresas, en lugar de que les retengan, están obligadas o autorizadas a autorretenerse renta e ICA sobre sus propias ventas; en ese caso, el asiento de causación de la venta debe incluir la autorretención practicada por la misma empresa vendedora. Contribuyentes del régimen simple de tributación: en general no son sujetos de retención en la fuente a título de renta por parte de sus clientes (con algunas excepciones), aunque sí pueden generar IVA si son responsables de este impuesto. Operaciones inferiores a la base mínima: si el valor de la compra o el servicio no supera la base mínima en UVT, no debe practicarse retefuente ni reteICA, aunque sí puede generarse IVA si la operación está gravada. Errores comunes al causar facturas con IVA y retenciones Calcular la retención en la fuente sobre el valor total de la factura (base más IVA) en lugar de sobre la base gravable. Calcular la reteIVA sobre el valor de la operación en lugar de sobre el valor del IVA generado. Aplicar tarifas de no declarante a un proveedor que sí es declarante de renta, o viceversa, sin haber verificado su situación tributaria. No verificar si la operación supera la base mínima antes de aplicar una retención. Registrar las retenciones que el cliente te practica en una venta como un gasto, cuando en realidad son un activo (anticipo de impuestos). Confundir la retención en la fuente con la reteICA municipal, aplicando una sola tarifa genérica sin consultar el acuerdo del municipio correspondiente. No emitir o solicitar el certificado de retención correspondiente para poder soportar el anticipo de impuestos ante la DIAN. Preguntas frecuentes sobre la causación de facturas con IVA y retenciones ¿La reteIVA se suma o se resta del valor de la factura? Se resta, junto con la retefuente y la reteICA cuando apliquen, del valor que finalmente recibirá el vendedor; ninguna de las retenciones reduce el ingreso ni el IVA generado que se declaran ante la DIAN, solo afecta el flujo de caja. ¿Todas las empresas deben practicar reteIVA? No. Solo quienes califican como agentes de retención de IVA según el artículo 437-2 del Estatuto Tributario están obligados a practicarla; el resto de compradores, aunque sean responsables de IVA, no necesariamente son agentes de retención de este impuesto. ¿Qué pasa si no se registra correctamente la retención que me practicaron? Si el certificado de retención no coincide con lo registrado en la contabilidad, la empresa puede tener diferencias al momento de descontar esos anticipos en su declaración de renta o de IVA, lo que puede generar glosas o requerimientos de la DIAN. Referencias Estatuto Tributario, artículos 365 a 419 — Retención en la fuente a título de renta. Estatuto Tributario, artículo 437-2 — Agentes de retención del IVA. Decreto 1625 de 2016 (Único Reglamentario en Materia Tributaria), modificado por el Decreto 572 de 2025 — Bases mínimas y tarifas de retención en la fuente. Decreto 2650 de 1993 — Plan Único de Cuentas (PUC). Resolución DIAN 000238 de 2025 — Valor de la UVT para el año gravable 2026. Resolución Unificada DIAN 000227 de 2025 — Sistema de facturación electrónica. Portal oficial de la DIAN: dian.gov.co
